The component's filter planner should classify each predicate as 'indexed label', 'arbitrary predicate', or 'highly selective' and route to the matching strategy (label-aware graph, predicate traversal, or brute-force over the filtered set).
papers.verification_evidence: no arXiv identifier; needs venue-page check

papers.title: Query Expansion by Prompting Large Language Models
papers.authors: Rolf Jagerman, Honglei Zhuang, Zhen Qin, Xuanhui Wang, Michael Bendersky
papers.citation_signal: The standard comparison of LLM query-expansion prompt styles (Q2D, Q2E, CoT, with and without pseudo-relevance feedback) and the paper that established chain-of-thought expansion for BM25; frequently cited alongside Query2doc and HyDE.
papers.key_contribution: Compares zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompts for generating query expansions (pseudo-documents, keyword lists, reasoning traces) against classical pseudo-relevance feedback on MS MARCO and BEIR with BM25. Chain-of-thought prompts are especially effective because the model decomposes the query step by step and emits many related terms; LLM-generated expansions outperform traditional PRF-based expansion.
papers.design_implication: The dossier's query-expansion technique offers only Query2doc and HyDE; add a CoT-expansion variant for the lexical channel and treat classical PRF (RM3) as the zero-cost baseline that any LLM expansion must beat on the golden set. Strip answer-like boilerplate from CoT outputs before concatenation and keep the original query repeated, as in Query2doc, so expansion terms cannot dominate.

papers.title: SPLADE-v3: New Baselines for SPLADE
papers.authors: Carlos Lassance, Hervé Déjean, Thibault Formal, Stéphane Clinchant
papers.citation_signal: Release note for the current SPLADE checkpoints (splade-v3, splade-v3-distilbert, splade-v3-doc) that supersede the SPLADE++ ED checkpoint the dossier recommends; adopted as the learned-sparse baseline in 2024-2025 reranking papers.
papers.key_contribution: Describes training changes in the latest SPLADE library and the SPLADE-v3 model family. A meta-analysis over more than 40 query sets shows SPLADE-v3 is statistically significantly more effective than both BM25 and SPLADE++, and comparable to cross-encoder rerankers; it exceeds 40 MRR@10 on MS MARCO dev and improves out-of-domain BEIR results by about 2%.
papers.design_implication: Update the dossier's learned-sparse default from SPLADE++ CoCondenser-EnsembleDistil (38.0 MRR@10) to SPLADE-v3 (>40 MRR@10, +2% BEIR) and note the document-only variant (splade-v3-doc) that needs no query-time encoder, which removes the GPU forward pass per query that the dossier lists as SPLADE's main latency cost.

papers.title: BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
papers.authors: Hongjin Su et al. (15 authors)
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2025; now the standard benchmark for reasoning-intensive retrieval and the evaluation target for the 2025 generation of reasoning rerankers (Rank1, ReasonIR, Rank-R1); exposes a failure mode BEIR/MTEB do not measure.
papers.key_contribution: About 1,400 real queries across domains such as economics, psychology, mathematics and coding whose relevant documents cannot be found by surface matching. The top MTEB model at the time (SFR-Embedding-Mistral, 59.0 MTEB) drops to about 18 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT. Adding LLM-generated reasoning about the query before retrieval improves results by up to 12.2 points, and feeding retrieved documents from the best retriever improves downstream QA by over 6.6 points.
papers.design_implication: Engineering queries ('which requirement is violated by this failure mode?') are often reasoning-intensive, so the golden set should include a BRIGHT-style slice; when first-stage scores are flat on such queries, the router should enable reasoning-based query expansion (an LLM writes the inferred technical need before retrieval) and a reasoning reranker, since embedding-leaderboard rank does not predict performance on this slice.

papers.title: Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking in Information Retrieval
papers.authors: Orion Weller, Kathryn Ricci, Eugene Yang, Andrew Yates, Dawn Lawrie, Benjamin Van Durme
papers.citation_signal: Semantic Scholar reports 87 citations within a year; COLM 2025; the first open reasoning reranker and the reference point for the 2025-2026 wave of 'thinking' rerankers (ReasonRR, Rank-R1, Qwen3-Reranker-style models).
papers.key_contribution: Trains a pointwise reranker that reasons before judging relevance by distilling more than 600,000 DeepSeek-R1 reasoning traces over MS MARCO query-passage pairs (dataset released). The resulting models produce inspectable reasoning chains usable by users or RAG systems, perform strongly on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as BRIGHT, and retain most of their quality when quantized, reducing compute and memory.
papers.design_implication: Adds a third reranker tier for reasoning-heavy, high-value queries (root-cause search, compliance questions) where cross-encoders fail; it is pointwise, so it batches and caches like a cross-encoder but at LLM cost, and its reasoning trace can be surfaced to the Answer Verification model as evidence. Gate it by the planner's budget and by a 'reasoning-intensive' query classifier.

papers.title: MMTEB: Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark
papers.authors: Kenneth Enevoldsen, Isaac Chung, Niklas Muennighoff, et al. (large community author list)
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2025; the current version of the MTEB leaderboard (MTEB v2 / MTEB(Multilingual), MTEB(eng, v2), MTEB(Code)) that practitioners actually consult in 2025-2026, superseding the 2022 MTEB paper the dossier cites.
papers.key_contribution: Community-driven expansion of MTEB to over 500 quality-controlled tasks across 250+ languages, adding instruction following, long-document retrieval and code retrieval. Finds that multi-billion-parameter LLM embedders reach state of the art on some subsets but the best public model overall is multilingual-e5-large-instruct at only 560M parameters. Introduces cheaper benchmark variants by downsampling tasks via inter-task correlation and by sampling hard negatives for retrieval, including a new zero-shot English benchmark that preserves model ordering at a fraction of the cost.
papers.design_implication: Shortlist embedding models from MTEB(eng, v2)/MTEB(Multilingual)/MTEB(Code) rather than the 2022 leaderboard, prefer the zero-shot subsets to avoid models trained on the benchmark, and reuse its hard-negative-sampled retrieval splits as a template for building cheap in-domain evaluation sets; the finding that a 560M model is the best public model argues against defaulting to 7B embedders.

papers.title: Qwen3 Embedding: Advancing Text Embedding and Reranking Through Foundation Models
papers.authors: Yanzhao Zhang, Mingxin Li, Dingkun Long, Xin Zhang, et al. (Qwen team, Alibaba)
papers.citation_signal: Ranked No. 1 on the MTEB multilingual leaderboard at release (June 2025) with a 70.58 score; the current default open embedding/reranker family (0.6B/4B/8B) in vLLM, Ollama, LlamaIndex and vector-DB integrations; successor to the GTE-Qwen models in the dossier's GTE entry.
papers.key_contribution: A family of embedding and reranking models (0.6B, 4B, 8B each) built on Qwen3 backbones with a multi-stage pipeline: large-scale unsupervised contrastive pre-training on LLM-synthesized data, supervised fine-tuning on high-quality labeled data, and model merging for robustness. The 8B embedder reports 70.58 on MTEB Multilingual and 80.68 on MTEB Code; the 8B reranker improves ranking over the 0.6B by about 3.0 points across tasks. Released under Apache 2.0.
papers.design_implication: Provides open, commercially usable embedders and rerankers at three cost tiers from one family, which maps directly onto the dossier's 'cpu-only / gpu / api' deployment profiles (0.6B on CPU, 4B-8B on GPU). The reranker is an instruction-following pointwise LLM scorer, so it slots into the cross-encoder adapter; validate on the in-domain golden set before replacing BERT-class rerankers, since the gain over MiniLM/bge-reranker is task dependent.

papers.title: Late Chunking: Contextual Chunk Embeddings Using Long-Context Embedding Models
papers.authors: Michael Günther, Isabelle Mohr, Daniel James Williams, Bo Wang, Han Xiao
papers.citation_signal: Implemented in Jina embeddings v3, Weaviate and LlamaIndex integrations; the main training-free alternative to Anthropic's LLM-generated contextual chunk headers for solving chunk context loss.
papers.key_contribution: Instead of embedding each chunk independently, run a long-context embedding model over the whole document (or an 8k-token window), then split the token-level outputs into chunks just before mean pooling, so each chunk embedding carries information from surrounding text. Improves results across several retrieval tasks with no additional training, applies to any long-context embedding model, and a dedicated fine-tuning method improves it further.
papers.design_implication: Offers a cheaper substitute for the dossier's LLM-generated contextual headers on the dense channel: no generation cost, one long-context forward pass per document. It does not help the BM25 channel (no text is added), so combine late chunking for embeddings with lightweight metadata/title prefixes for the lexical index, and A/B both against Anthropic-style headers on the top-20 failure-rate metric.

techniques.name: Tuned BM25 / BM25F lexical first stage
techniques.description: Index chunk text (plus title, section path, and generated context) in an inverted index. Score with BM25: for each query term t, IDF(t) * tf*(k1+1) / (tf + k1*(1 - b + b*dl/avgdl)). For multi-field engineering documents use BM25F: compute a per-document pseudo-frequency by summing field term frequencies weighted by per-field boosts (title, heading, identifier fields high; body 1.0), then apply the saturation once. Keep a dedicated analyzer for identifiers (part numbers, error codes, requirement IDs, function names): lowercase, keep punctuation-joined tokens (e.g. 'ERR_1203', 'A320-NEO'), and emit both the whole identifier and its sub-tokens. Return the top-N (N = fusion window, default 200-1000) with raw scores.
source_titles: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
A Replication Study of Dense Passage Retriever
Introducing Contextual Retrieval
techniques.when_to_use: Always, as one channel of the hybrid. Dominant when queries contain exact identifiers, rare technical terms, or the corpus is out of domain for the embedding model (BEIR: dense models averaged below BM25 zero-shot).
techniques.tradeoffs: Vocabulary mismatch (synonyms, paraphrase) is not handled; fix with SPLADE, query expansion or the dense channel. Very cheap: ~20 ms CPU per query on 1M documents, 0.4 GB index (BEIR Table 3). An under-tuned BM25 baseline hides hybrid gains (Ma et al. 2021).
techniques.default_parameters: k1 in [1.2, 2.0] and b = 0.75 as the long-standing defaults discussed in Robertson & Zaragoza's parameter-optimisation chapter; grid-search k1 in {0.6..2.0} and b in {0.3..1.0} on an in-domain dev set (Ma et al. show the tuned baseline differs by ~4 points top-20 accuracy). Candidate depth for fusion: 1000 (Ma et al.), or 150-200 when a reranker follows (Anthropic used 150).

techniques.name: Dense bi-encoder retrieval with instruction prefixes and HNSW ANN
techniques.description: Choose an embedding model from the MTEB/BEIR retrieval leaderboard (E5/BGE/GTE class, 110M-335M params by default). Encode documents once with the model's document prefix ('passage: ' for E5; none or instruction for BGE docs) and queries with the query prefix/instruction ('query: ' for E5; 'Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: '-style instruction for BGE). Normalize vectors and use cosine/dot product. Index with HNSW (FAISS, hnswlib, or the vector DB's HNSW). Retrieve top-N with scores. Keep a model registry keyed by (model_id, prefix_scheme, dimension, normalization) and store it with the index so re-embedding is triggered on model change.
source_titles: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (E5)
C-Pack: Packed Resources For General Chinese Embeddings (BGE)
Towards General Text Embeddings with Multi-stage Contrastive Learning (GTE)
MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning (Contriever)
techniques.when_to_use: Always, as the semantic channel; critical for paraphrased natural-language questions and cross-lingual queries. Alone it is sufficient only in-domain with fine-tuning; otherwise fuse.
techniques.tradeoffs: 3 GB per 1M passages at 768-dim fp32 (BEIR), 14-20 ms GPU / 125-275 ms CPU per query; zero-shot ranking quality can trail BM25 (Contriever nDCG@10 36.0 vs 41.7) although recall@100 is competitive; single vectors have bounded capacity for long documents (Luan et al.), so keep chunks short.
techniques.default_parameters: Chunk 200-400 tokens; HNSW M = 32-64 (DPR used 512 neighbours in FAISS HNSW), efConstruction = 200, efSearch = 128 (DPR), raise efSearch until Recall@100 vs flat search >= 0.98; retrieve top-100 to top-1000 for fusion. Use E5/BGE/GTE-base (110M) as default, -large (335M) when GPU budget allows, LLM-backbone (7B, RepLLaMA-style) only for small high-value corpora. Always apply the model's prefixes.

techniques.name: Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE / SPLADE++) as the expansion-aware lexical channel
techniques.description: Run a SPLADE++ encoder over each chunk: for every input token, take the MLM-head logits over the 30,522-term vocabulary, apply log(1+ReLU(.)), max-pool over tokens to get one weight per vocabulary term, and store the non-zero (term, weight) pairs in an inverted index (impact-ordered postings). Encode the query the same way (stronger sparsity). Score = dot product of query and document sparse vectors, executed by the inverted index. Optionally combine with BM25 in the same index as a second field.
source_titles: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking
From Distillation to Hard Negative Sampling: Making Sparse Neural IR Models More Effective (SPLADE++)
RankZephyr: Effective and Robust Zero-Shot Listwise Reranking is a Breeze!
techniques.when_to_use: When you want dense-level zero-shot quality (BEIR 50.5-50.7 vs 43.7 BM25, 49.7 ColBERTv2) while keeping inverted-index infrastructure, interpretability (visible term weights), and synonym expansion for the lexical side. Excellent first stage before an LLM reranker (RankZephyr's setup).
techniques.tradeoffs: Requires a GPU/CPU forward pass per query (~BERT-base cost) and a learned model that is MS MARCO-trained (domain gap possible); document expansion increases postings vs BM25; latency depends on sparsity (FLOPS regularizer).
techniques.default_parameters: Use the released SPLADE++ CoCondenser-EnsembleDistil checkpoint (MS MARCO MRR@10 38.0). If training: FLOPS lambda in [1e-4, 1e-1], ramped quadratically to step 50k, lambda_q > lambda_d; target ~18 non-zero terms/doc and ~6/query for the most efficient setting (MRR@10 0.296) or looser sparsity for ~0.32-0.38. Fuse its top-1000 with the dense channel.

techniques.name: Multi-vector late interaction (ColBERTv2 + PLAID) as a precision-oriented retriever/reranker
techniques.description: Encode each chunk into per-token 128-dim vectors; cluster all token vectors into K centroids (K = nearest power of two above 16*sqrt(#token embeddings)); store each vector as centroid id + 2-bit residual (~36 bytes). At query time (32 query tokens incl. [MASK] augmentation), PLAID: (1) find nearest centroids per query token, (2) score candidate passages by centroid interaction, (3) prune to ndocs, (4) decompress residuals only for survivors and compute exact MaxSim = sum over query tokens of max cosine to any passage token. Can be used end-to-end or to rerank a fused candidate list (cheaper than a cross-encoder: 61 ms vs 10,700 ms for BERT-base on 1000 candidates in the original ColBERT).
source_titles: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction
PLAID: An Efficient Engine for Late Interaction Retrieval
Sparse, Dense, and Attentional Representations for Text Retrieval
techniques.when_to_use: Long technical passages (specifications, standards clauses, log excerpts, code) where token-level matching matters and single vectors saturate; as a middle tier when cross-encoder latency is unaffordable; when out-of-domain robustness is required (LoTTE Success@5 71.6 vs 48.3 BM25).
techniques.tradeoffs: Index is 6-10x larger than single-vector (16-25 GiB for 8.8M MS MARCO passages even compressed; 154 GiB uncompressed); needs the PLAID engine; indexing is GPU-heavy (hours on 4 GPUs for 8.8M passages). Latency tens of ms GPU, tens-hundreds ms CPU.
techniques.default_parameters: dim = 128, query max length 32 tokens (raise to 64-128 for long engineering queries), 2-bit residuals, nbits=2; PLAID ncells = 4-8 centroids per query token, ndocs = 1024 candidates before exact scoring, centroid_score_threshold ~0.45-0.5 (tune for latency); rerank window 100-1000.

techniques.name: Rank fusion: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (zero-config) and normalized convex combination (tuned)
techniques.description: Collect top-N lists L_1..L_m from each channel. RRF: score(d) = sum_i 1/(k + rank_i(d)) over lists containing d; sort descending. Convex combination (CC): normalize each channel's scores with theoretical min-max (divide by the channel's theoretical range, e.g. cosine in [-1,1] -> [0,1]; for BM25 use observed min-max over the top-N or an empirical upper bound), then score(d) = alpha*s_dense(d) + (1-alpha)*s_lexical(d), with missing scores treated as that channel's minimum (0). For m > 2 channels generalize to a weight vector summing to 1. Fit alpha by grid search in steps of 0.05 maximizing nDCG@10 on a dev set of judged queries; re-fit per collection. Deduplicate by canonical chunk id before fusion; optionally collapse multiple chunks of one parent document (keep max) after fusion.
source_titles: Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods
An Analysis of Fusion Functions for Hybrid Retrieval
A Replication Study of Dense Passage Retriever
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) retriever - Elasticsearch reference
Unlocking the Power of Hybrid Search - A Deep Dive into Weaviate's Fusion Algorithms
techniques.when_to_use: Whenever two or more channels run. RRF when no labelled queries exist or channel scores are incomparable (e.g. a third-party API returns ranks only). CC once >= 30-50 judged queries exist (Bruch: alpha converges with <5% of training data) and when score gaps carry information (Weaviate: +6% recall on FiQA).
techniques.tradeoffs: RRF discards score magnitude and its constant does not transfer when tuned (MS MARCO-tuned (10,4) dropped HotpotQA nDCG from 0.675 to 0.621); CC requires calibration data and score normalization and can be skewed by a channel with heavy-tailed scores. Both are O(m*N) and negligible in latency.
techniques.default_parameters: RRF k = 60 (Cormack et al.; Elasticsearch rank_constant default 60); rank_window_size = max(requested size, 100), 1000 when a reranker is not used; equal channel weights. CC: alpha (semantic weight) = 0.7 default, search [0.5, 0.9]; Bruch found alpha = 0.8 best with [0.6, 0.8] consistently good; Ma et al. found BM25 weight 0.55 on raw DPR scores / 1.30 normalized via grid over [0,2] step 0.05. Theoretical min-max normalization.

techniques.name: Cross-encoder / monoT5 pointwise reranking of the fused pool
techniques.description: For each (query, candidate) pair in the fused top-K, run a cross-encoder (MiniLM/DeBERTa/bge-reranker/Cohere Rerank) or a seq2seq model prompted as 'Query: {q} Document: {d} Relevant:' and take softmax over only the 'true'/'false' token logits as P(relevant). Truncate each document to the model's window (512 tokens for BERT-class; 4,093 or 32,764 for Cohere v3/v4) keeping the generated context/title first. Sort by score; apply an optional relevance threshold calibrated per domain; return top-k' (5-20) with scores and original channel provenance.
source_titles: Passage Re-ranking with BERT (monoBERT)
Document Ranking with a Pretrained Sequence-to-Sequence Model (monoT5)
BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
Introducing Contextual Retrieval
Reranking Best Practices - Cohere documentation
techniques.when_to_use: Nearly always before passing context to a generator: it is the largest generalizable quality gain (BEIR +11% over BM25, best on 16/18 datasets; Anthropic: failure rate 2.9% -> 1.9%). Skip only for ultra-low-latency autocomplete-style use.
techniques.tradeoffs: 450 ms GPU / 6,100 ms CPU for BM25+CE over 1M docs in BEIR vs 20 ms for BM25; cost scales linearly with K; truncation can hide the relevant span in long documents; scores are query-dependent (not comparable across queries) so thresholds must be calibrated.
techniques.default_parameters: Rerank depth K = 100 (research default; RankGPT/RankZephyr) or 150 (Anthropic) and return top 20 to the generator (20 beat 5 and 10 in Anthropic's test); K = 1000 for offline/batch. Default model: monoT5-base/3B-class or bge-reranker-large/MiniLM-L12 cross-encoder for online, monoT5-3B for offline. Threshold: mean score of 30-50 borderline (query, doc) pairs (Cohere procedure). Max 512 tokens per passage for BERT-class rerankers.

techniques.name: Listwise LLM reranking with sliding windows (RankGPT / RankZephyr), optionally distilled
techniques.description: Take the top-K candidates (K = 100, from the fused + optionally cross-encoder-reranked list). Starting from the bottom, present a window of w passages, each tagged [1]..[w] and truncated to ~300 tokens, and ask the LLM to output a permutation of identifiers ordered by relevance; parse the permutation, slide the window up by stride s, and repeat so top candidates bubble upward; run p passes if desired. Use an open 7B model (RankZephyr) on-prem or a frontier API model; to reduce cost, use the cheaper model for the full K and the expensive model only on its top-30. For online latency, distill the permutations into a 400M cross-encoder (RankNet loss over LLM-generated orderings).
source_titles: Is ChatGPT Good at Search? Investigating Large Language Models as Re-Ranking Agents (RankGPT)
RankZephyr: Effective and Robust Zero-Shot Listwise Reranking is a Breeze!
Fine-Tuning LLaMA for Multi-Stage Text Retrieval (RepLLaMA / RankLLaMA)
techniques.when_to_use: High-value or offline queries (evaluation set construction, incident post-mortem search, compliance review), building training labels for a cheaper reranker, or when zero-shot quality on novel domains must be maximal (GPT-4 nDCG@10 75.59 vs monoT5-3B 71.83 on DL19; RankZephyr 0.78/0.82 on DL19/DL20).
techniques.tradeoffs: ~11 s (gpt-3.5) to ~32 s (gpt-4) and $0.04-$0.60 per query at K = 100 (RankGPT); sensitive to window prompt formatting; proprietary models raise confidentiality concerns for engineering data (mitigated by RankZephyr on-prem). Distillation needs ~10K queries (~$40 of gpt-3.5 labels in RankGPT).
techniques.default_parameters: window w = 20, stride s = 10, K = 100 (RankGPT, RankZephyr defaults), 1 pass online / 3 passes offline (RankZephyr-rho); two-tier: cheap model over 100, strong model over its top-30 (~1/5 the cost of strong-only); passage truncation ~300 tokens; temperature 0.

techniques.name: LLM query expansion and hypothetical documents (HyDE / Query2doc), router-gated and cached
techniques.description: Query2doc (lexical channel): few-shot (k = 4) prompt an LLM to write a pseudo-document answering the query; form q' = concat(q repeated 5 times, pseudo_doc); run BM25/SPLADE on q'. HyDE (dense channel): prompt an instruction-following LLM 'Write a passage that answers: {q}' N times (temperature > 0), embed each generated passage with the document encoder, average the N vectors (optionally with the real query embedding as an N+1th vector), and search the dense index with the averaged vector. Gate both behind a router that fires only when (a) the query is short/ambiguous, (b) first-stage top score dispersion is low, or (c) the task decomposer flags an exploratory sub-question; cache expansions by normalized query string.
source_titles: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)
Query2doc: Query Expansion with Large Language Models
Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning (Contriever)
techniques.when_to_use: Zero-shot or new-domain deployments with no fine-tuned retriever (HyDE: DL19 nDCG@10 44.5 -> 61.3 over Contriever, Recall@1k 88.0 beating fine-tuned models; Query2doc: BM25 DL19 51.2 -> 66.2). Not worth it on top of a strong distilled dense retriever (Query2doc gains shrink to +0.4-0.8 MRR).
techniques.tradeoffs: >2,000 ms LLM latency vs 16 ms BM25 (Query2doc), ~$55k for 550k calls; hallucinated expansions can steer retrieval toward plausible-but-wrong content, especially for proprietary identifiers the LLM has never seen; HyDE's instruction may be under-specified for some domains (FiQA, DBPedia underperformed Contriever-FT).
techniques.default_parameters: Query2doc: k = 4 few-shot examples, query repeated 5x, pseudo-doc <= 128 tokens. HyDE: N = 4-8 hypothetical documents (paper leaves N unspecified; averaging requires N > 1), include the query embedding as an extra vector, temperature 0.7, small fast model. Cache TTL hours-days keyed on normalized query; router threshold: fire when top-1/top-10 fused-score ratio < 1.2 or query length < 6 tokens.

techniques.name: Index-time enrichment: contextual chunk headers and filtered generative expansion
techniques.description: At ingestion, for each chunk, call an LLM with the (prompt-cached) full parent document and the chunk, asking for a 50-100-token statement situating the chunk (document title, section, entity, time period, product/revision); prepend it to the chunk text used for both the embedding and the BM25/SPLADE index while keeping the raw chunk for display. Optionally also generate 3-10 synthetic queries per chunk (doc2query) and append them to the lexical field, but first score each (query, chunk) pair with a cross-encoder and drop those below a relevance threshold (Doc2Query--). Store provenance (generator model, prompt version) so enrichment can be regenerated when models change.
source_titles: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
Document Expansion by Query Prediction (doc2query)
Doc2Query--: When Less is More
Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
techniques.when_to_use: Corpora where chunks lose meaning without their parent (specifications with numbered clauses, tables, incident timelines, BOM rows, code functions without file/module context). Anthropic: top-20 failure rate 5.7% -> 2.9% with contextual embeddings + contextual BM25; Doc2Query--: up to +16% effectiveness, -23% query time, -33% index size vs unfiltered expansion.
techniques.tradeoffs: One-time LLM cost (~$1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching for 800-token chunks); re-ingestion needed when prompts/models change; unfiltered generation injects hallucinated terms (Doc2Query--).
techniques.default_parameters: Chunk 200-800 tokens (Anthropic used 800 in cost estimate; Chroma/Qu et al. favour 200-400 for precision), context 50-100 tokens, small/fast LLM with prompt caching; doc2query 5 queries per chunk, keep only those with cross-encoder P(relevant) >= 0.5 (or top 70% by score); always prefix the document title (DPR).

techniques.name: Chunking and multi-granularity indexing with parent-child references
techniques.description: Split documents with a recursive, boundary-aware splitter (section headings -> paragraphs -> sentences) targeting a token budget, no or minimal overlap. Store each chunk with parent_doc_id, section_path, ordinal, char offsets, and structured metadata. Optionally build a finer child index (sentences or LLM-extracted propositions) whose hits are mapped back to the parent chunk returned to the generator ('small-to-big'). Treat chunk size, overlap, and granularity as per-collection configuration tied to the embedding model version. Evaluate with token-level IoU/recall against span-labelled queries.
source_titles: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval
Is Semantic Chunking Worth the Computational Cost?
Dense X Retrieval: What Retrieval Granularity Should We Use?
Sparse, Dense, and Attentional Representations for Text Retrieval
techniques.when_to_use: Every corpus; proposition/sentence child indexes when queries target specific facts in dense technical prose (Dense X: Recall@5 +9.3 for Contriever, QA EM +2.7 to +4.1 at fixed token budget); semantic chunkers only for multi-topic concatenated documents (Qu et al.).
techniques.tradeoffs: Smaller chunks improve precision/IoU but lower recall per chunk and multiply index size (propositions ~6x passages); overlap adds redundant tokens the generator pays for; semantic/LLM chunking is slow (seconds to tens of minutes per corpus in Chroma's tests) with inconsistent gains.
techniques.default_parameters: RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter at 200-400 tokens, overlap 0 (Chroma: 200/0 gave recall 88.1, precision 7.0; 400/0 recall 89.5; 800/400 worst IoU); overlap 10-25% only with small-context embedders (all-MiniLM preferred 250/125); return the parent chunk or a 2-3 chunk window around hits; max 5-20 chunks to the generator.

techniques.name: Metadata-filtered hybrid retrieval and structured-record serialization
techniques.description: Attach structured metadata to every chunk (project, system/component, document type, revision/version, date, severity, author/team, language, file path, standard clause id). Translate the task prompt's constraints into filters (via the task decomposition/planner step or a small schema-guided LLM call) and push them into each channel: inverted-index filter clauses for BM25/SPLADE; filtered HNSW (ACORN-style predicate-aware traversal, or the vector DB's native pre-filter) for dense; apply the same filter to late-interaction candidates. For record-like sources (BOM lines, incident tickets, test results) serialize to ordered 'key: value' text with the most discriminative fields first before embedding and reranking, and keep the raw record for display.
source_titles: ACORN: Performant and Predicate-Agnostic Search Over Vector Embeddings and Structured Data
Reranking Best Practices - Cohere documentation
The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
techniques.when_to_use: Any engineering corpus: queries are routinely scoped ('in release 4.2', 'for the hydraulic subsystem', 'incidents last quarter'); multi-tenant or access-controlled deployments where filtering is a security boundary.
techniques.tradeoffs: Post-filtering the top-k of an unfiltered ANN search collapses recall for selective predicates; pre-filtering with naive HNSW can disconnect the graph; ACORN or pre-filter+brute-force fallbacks fix this at some index/maintenance cost. Serialization order matters because rerankers truncate long records.
techniques.default_parameters: Pre-filter when predicate selectivity < ~10% of the collection (fall back to brute-force scan over the filtered set when it is < ~10k vectors); ACORN reports 2-1,000x throughput at fixed recall vs prior methods. Keep records under the reranker window (512 tokens BERT-class; 4,093 Cohere v3) with 5-8 priority fields first; always include a human-readable title line.

techniques.name: BEIR-style evaluation harness with regression gates
techniques.description: Build an in-domain golden set: 100-500 queries sampled from real logs plus task-decomposer-generated sub-questions, with graded relevance judgments (0-3) over pooled results from all channels and the reranker (depth 20-50) judged by domain experts, optionally pre-labelled by an LLM judge and verified. Compute nDCG@10, Recall@{20,100,1000}, MRR@10 per channel, per fusion setting and end-to-end, with paired significance tests. Store results per (index version, model registry version, fusion params). Run as CI: fail if nDCG@10 drops > 1 point or Recall@100 drops > 2 points relative to the pinned baseline. Also track latency p50/p95 and cost per 1k queries per stage.
source_titles: BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
Pyserini: An Easy-to-Use Python Toolkit to Support Replicable IR Research with Sparse and Dense Representations
Cumulated Gain-Based Evaluation of IR Techniques
CoIR: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Code Information Retrieval Models
techniques.when_to_use: Before every model swap, fusion-parameter change, chunking change or index rebuild; mandatory for choosing alpha/k and reranker depth.
techniques.tradeoffs: Judgment collection is the main cost; pooled judgments bias toward systems in the pool (re-judge new systems' unjudged top-k); LLM judges correlate with but do not replace expert labels on specialized engineering content.
techniques.default_parameters: nDCG@10 primary; Recall@100 for first-stage headroom; MRR@10 for single-answer tasks; pool depth 20 per system; graded 4-point scale (Järvelin & Kekäläinen); >= 100 queries for stable alpha fitting (Bruch: <5% of data suffices); regression tolerance 1.0 nDCG@10 point; report BM25 baseline alongside every hybrid result (Ma et al.).

techniques.name: In-domain adaptation without labels: synthetic query generation + cross-encoder pseudo-labels + ANN hard-negative mining
techniques.description: Cold-start recipe for a new collection. (1) Sample passages from the collection; for each, generate q synthetic queries with an LLM prompted with 3-8 expert-written (query, passage) examples in the collection's query style (Promptagator), or with a T5 doc2query generator (GPL). (2) Round-trip filter: keep a synthetic query only if a current retriever ranks its source passage at rank 1 (or within top-k). (3) Mine hard negatives for each query from the current dense index (ANCE-style, refreshing the negative index from a recent checkpoint every few thousand steps) and from BM25. (4) Pseudo-label each (query, positive, negative) with the component's cross-encoder and train the bi-encoder with a margin-MSE loss on the score differences (GPL), or fine-tune the cross-encoder itself with a listwise softmax loss over groups (RankT5). (5) Register the adapted models as collection-specific registry entries and re-run the golden-set evaluation before promotion.
source_titles: GPL: Generative Pseudo Labeling for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation of Dense Retrieval
Promptagator: Few-shot Dense Retrieval From 8 Examples
Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning for Dense Text Retrieval (ANCE)
RankT5: Fine-Tuning T5 for Text Ranking with Ranking Losses
techniques.when_to_use: Every new engineering collection whose queries differ from web search (identifier-heavy, clause references, log text), before any real query logs exist; also to refresh models when the golden set shows the MS MARCO-trained embedder trailing BM25.
techniques.tradeoffs: One-off generation cost (one LLM/T5 call per passage times q) and a training job per collection; synthetic queries inherit generator biases, so the round-trip filter and expert examples are essential; ANN-mined negatives include unlabeled positives (false negatives), which the cross-encoder pseudo-labels mitigate. GPL reports up to +9.3 nDCG@10 over an off-the-shelf dense retriever; Promptagator reports +1.2 nDCG@10 over ColBERTv2 with 8 examples and a further ~5 points from a reranker trained on the same data.
techniques.default_parameters: q = 3 synthetic queries per passage (GPL's setting); 8 few-shot examples per task (Promptagator); round-trip filter requiring the source passage at rank 1; negatives: 50 per query mixed from dense ANN and BM25, negative index refreshed every 10k steps (ANCE used asynchronous refresh); margin-MSE distillation from the cross-encoder; listwise group size 8-32 for RankT5-style reranker fine-tuning; stop when golden-set nDCG@10 stops improving.

techniques.name: Pairwise and setwise LLM reranking with sorting (alternative to listwise sliding windows)
techniques.description: Pairwise (PRP): prompt 'Given query q, which passage is more relevant, A or B?'; evaluate both orders to cancel position bias; aggregate with (a) all-pairs win counts for small k, (b) a sorting algorithm using the LLM as comparator, or (c) sliding-window bubble passes that promote the best candidate to the top each pass (PRP-Sliding-K, linear in k per pass). Setwise: prompt with a set of c passages and ask for the single most relevant; use the answer as the comparator of a heap-sort (or bubble-sort) so that extracting the top-k needs O(k log n) set queries instead of O(n^2) pairs. Both avoid parsing long permutations and are robust to the initial order. Use logits over the identifier tokens (A/B or 1..c) rather than generated text when the model exposes them.
source_titles: Large Language Models are Effective Text Rankers with Pairwise Ranking Prompting (PRP)
A Setwise Approach for Effective and Highly Efficient Zero-shot Ranking with Large Language Models
Multi-Stage Document Ranking with BERT (monoBERT/duoBERT)
techniques.when_to_use: On-prem reranking with moderate open models (PRP matched GPT-4 listwise with a 20B Flan-UL2), when only the top-10/20 needs to be exact, or when listwise permutation parsing fails frequently (small models, long passages).
techniques.tradeoffs: Pairwise all-pairs is O(n^2) LLM calls; sliding/sorting variants cut this to O(k n) or O(n log n) but add sequential latency because comparisons depend on earlier results (less batchable than listwise windows). Setwise needs fewer calls and tokens than pairwise at similar effectiveness. Pointwise remains cheapest and most batchable but least effective (Setwise paper's systematic comparison).
techniques.default_parameters: PRP: sliding-window passes K = 10 to fix the top-10 over a top-20/30 candidate list, both orderings per pair; Setwise: set size c = 3-4 with heap sort, k = 10-20; candidates truncated to ~300 tokens; temperature 0; log inference count and prompt tokens per query. Fall back to listwise windows when the model exposes no logits and parsing succeeds >98% of the time.

techniques.name: Dimension truncation (Matryoshka) with shortlist-and-rescore, plus scalar/binary quantization
techniques.description: For embedding models trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning, store full vectors but build the ANN graph over the first d' dimensions (or int8/binary-quantized full vectors). At query time: (1) ANN search on truncated/quantized vectors with an oversampled shortlist (k_short = oversample x k), (2) rescore the shortlist with exact full-precision dot products loaded from disk or a secondary store, (3) return top-k. Record (model_id, d', quantization) in the model registry and in the index metadata; recompute the recall-vs-flat calibration whenever any of them changes.
source_titles: Matryoshka Representation Learning
Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs (HNSW)
Improving Text Embeddings with Large Language Models (E5-Mistral)
techniques.when_to_use: Large corpora (tens of millions of chunks) or LLM-backbone embedders with 1024-4096 dimensions where memory for the HNSW graph dominates cost; multi-tenant deployments where many small collections must stay memory-resident.
techniques.tradeoffs: Index memory and ANN latency shrink roughly linearly with d' (MRL reports up to 14x speedups via adaptive shortlisting) at a small recall loss that the rescoring step largely recovers; requires a model trained with MRL (truncating a non-MRL model degrades sharply); rescoring adds a random-access read per shortlist item. Binary quantization needs larger oversampling.
techniques.default_parameters: d' = 1/4 of full dimension (e.g. 256 of 1024) for the ANN pass; oversample 4x (k_short = 4k) before rescoring; int8 scalar quantization by default, binary only with >=10x oversampling; acceptance test: Recall@100 vs full-precision flat search >= 0.98 on the golden queries; HNSW M = 16-32, efSearch tuned upward until the acceptance test passes.

techniques.name: Single-model multi-representation hybrid (dense + learned-sparse + multi-vector from one encoder)
techniques.description: Run one forward pass of a multi-function embedder (BGE-M3 class) per chunk and per query to obtain (a) a normalized dense vector from the CLS/pooled output, (b) sparse lexical weights (ReLU-activated per-token weights max-pooled per vocabulary id) stored in an inverted index, and (c) per-token vectors for ColBERT-style MaxSim. Retrieve candidates with the dense and sparse heads, union them, then compute all three scores for every candidate and fuse with a weighted sum s = w_dense*s_dense + w_sparse*s_sparse + w_multi*s_multi (weights tuned on the dev set), optionally followed by the cross-encoder tier. Scores are produced by the same model so convex combination is well-posed without cross-model normalization.
source_titles: BGE M3-Embedding: Multi-Linguality, Multi-Functionality, Multi-Granularity Text Embeddings Through Self-Knowledge Distillation
An Analysis of Fusion Functions for Hybrid Retrieval
techniques.when_to_use: Multilingual or mixed-language corpora, long documents (up to 8k tokens), or deployments that want hybrid signals with a single encoder and a single GPU pass per query; a good default for the 'cpu-only' and 'gpu' profiles when SPLADE and ColBERT infrastructure is not available.
techniques.tradeoffs: One model's inductive biases drive all channels, so it does not provide the independence that BM25 brings (keep BM25 as a separate channel for identifiers and exact matches); the multi-vector head requires storing per-token vectors for candidates (use it only to rescore the union, not for retrieval, to avoid ColBERT-scale indexes); model is still MS MARCO/multilingual-trained and benefits from the adaptation technique above.
techniques.default_parameters: Dense and multi-vector weights 1.0, sparse weight lower (around 0.3) as a starting point, then grid-search on the dev set in steps of 0.1; retrieve top-200 from dense and top-200 from sparse, rescore the union with all three heads; max input 8,192 tokens but chunk at 512-1,024 for precision; keep BM25 as an additional channel fused with RRF or CC.

techniques.name: Late chunking for the dense channel (context-preserving chunk embeddings without generation)
techniques.description: At ingestion, feed the entire document (or a window of up to the embedding model's context, e.g. 8k tokens) through a long-context embedding model once, obtain per-token hidden states, then apply the chunk boundaries (from the same recursive splitter used for BM25) to those token states and mean-pool each span into its chunk embedding. Store the chunk embedding alongside the raw chunk text and the parent/child references. Documents longer than the context window are processed in overlapping macro-windows with the chunk assigned to the window where it is most central.
source_titles: Late Chunking: Contextual Chunk Embeddings Using Long-Context Embedding Models
Introducing Contextual Retrieval
techniques.when_to_use: Corpora whose chunks lose referents (pronouns, 'this clause', table rows) and where the LLM-generated contextual header cost (~$1 per million tokens plus re-ingestion on prompt changes) is unwanted; works with any mean-pooled long-context embedder (jina-embeddings-v3, nomic, bge-m3).
techniques.tradeoffs: Zero generation cost and no prompt versioning, but helps only the dense channel (BM25/SPLADE see no added text), requires a long-context mean-pooling model, and one long forward pass per document (attention cost grows with length). Gains are reported across several retrieval tasks but are smaller than LLM headers on corpora where the missing context is not present in the surrounding text at all (e.g. metadata-only context such as revision or product).
techniques.default_parameters: Macro-window = model context (8,192 tokens) with 10% overlap; chunk sizes as in the dossier (200-400 tokens, 0 overlap); mean pooling over token states (not CLS); still prefix the document title to the lexical field; A/B against LLM contextual headers on top-20 failure rate and adopt the cheaper one that meets the target.

techniques.name: Reasoning-aware retrieval path: query reasoning expansion + reasoning reranker, gated by a reasoning-intensity classifier
techniques.description: (1) Classify each (sub-)query as lexical/identifier, semantic, or reasoning-intensive (a small LLM call or a trained classifier on query logs; features: no identifiers, causal/comparative phrasing, low first-stage score dispersion). (2) For reasoning-intensive queries, prompt an LLM to write the inferred technical need and likely answer content (reasoning expansion), and run retrieval on both the original and expanded query, fusing the two result lists. (3) Rerank the fused top-k with a reasoning reranker (Rank1-class pointwise model that emits a reasoning trace followed by a relevance judgment; use the probability of the 'true' token as the score). (4) Pass the reasoning traces of the top passages to the verification stage as evidence. Cache the expansion and the reranker judgments by (query hash, chunk id).
source_titles: BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
Rank1: Test-Time Compute for Reranking in Information Retrieval
Query Expansion by Prompting Large Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Root-cause and 'what does this imply' queries over incident reports, standards and design rationale, where BRIGHT shows top MTEB embedders collapse (59.0 MTEB -> ~18 nDCG@10) and reasoning expansion adds up to 12.2 points; offline analysis, compliance review and golden-set construction.
techniques.tradeoffs: Both steps are LLM calls: expansion adds >1 s and reranking adds generation of reasoning tokens per candidate (seconds per query at depth 20-30 even with a 7B model), so it must be budget-gated; reasoning rerankers are pointwise and batchable but their traces inflate cost; quantized versions retain most quality (Rank1). Misclassifying lexical queries as reasoning-intensive wastes budget and can hurt identifier matching.
techniques.default_parameters: Classifier threshold tuned for <10% of traffic routed to the reasoning path initially; expansion with temperature 0 and a 200-token cap, original query retained and fused with the expanded-query run via RRF k=60; reasoning reranker depth 20-30 over the cross-encoder's top list; int8/4-bit quantized 7B reasoning reranker on-prem; cache TTL days.

techniques.name: Score-level fusion variants and fusion selection by channel capabilities (CombSUM / CombMNZ / RRF / CC)
techniques.description: Generalize the fusion module to the Fox & Shaw family: after per-channel normalization (theoretical min-max where the score range is known, observed min-max otherwise), compute CombSUM = sum of normalized scores (equal-weight convex combination), CombMNZ = CombSUM x (number of channels that returned the document), CombMAX, and keep RRF as the rank-only option. Choose the method from the channels' declared capabilities: if every channel returns comparable normalized scores and judged queries exist, use tuned convex combination; if scores exist but no judgments, use CombMNZ (its multiplicity bonus approximates the 'agreement is evidence' prior for weakly correlated channels); if any channel returns ranks only, use RRF. Always deduplicate by canonical chunk id before fusion and treat a document absent from a channel as having that channel's minimum normalized score.
source_titles: Combination of Multiple Searches (CombSUM / CombMNZ)
An Analysis of Fusion Functions for Hybrid Retrieval
BERT-based Dense Retrievers Require Interpolation with BM25 for Effective Passage Retrieval
Out-of-Domain Semantics to the Rescue! Zero-Shot Hybrid Retrieval Models
techniques.when_to_use: Whenever more than two channels are fused (BM25 + SPLADE + dense + multi-vector), where RRF's equal treatment of ranks discards the strong agreement signal, and in the no-judgment regime where tuned CC cannot be fitted but scores are available.
techniques.tradeoffs: CombMNZ rewards documents retrieved by many channels, which is right when channels are complementary and wrong when two channels are near-duplicates (e.g. two learned-sparse models), so use the channel taxonomy to avoid double counting; score-level methods are sensitive to normalization and outliers, rank-level RRF is not. All are O(m x N) and negligible in latency. Fox & Shaw found CombSUM significantly better than the best single run on TREC-2; Bruch et al. found tuned CC beats RRF on every dataset tested.
techniques.default_parameters: Normalization: theoretical min-max for cosine/dot-product channels, observed min-max over the top-N for BM25/SPLADE; CombMNZ as the default when scores exist but no judgments; switch to CC with alpha ~0.7-0.8 (semantic) once >=30-50 judged queries exist; RRF k=60 as the rank-only fallback; fusion window N = 100-1000 per channel; interpolate with BM25 even in-domain (Wang et al.).

techniques.name: Multi-stage cascade specification with per-stage candidate budgets (mono -> duo -> listwise)
techniques.description: Specify the pipeline as an ordered list of stages, each with (input_depth k_in, output_depth k_out, model, declared cost per candidate, declared latency). Stage 0: channels + fusion produce k_0 (100-1000). Stage 1: pointwise cross-encoder/monoT5/RankT5 scores k_0 and keeps k_1 (20-50). Stage 2 (optional): pairwise duo-style or setwise LLM comparisons over k_1 produce an exact top-k_2 (10-20). Stage 3 (optional, offline/high-value): listwise or reasoning LLM reranker over k_2. The planner solves for the deepest stage set whose summed declared latency and cost fit the caller's budget, and the cascade logs per-stage rank changes (Kendall tau between consecutive stages) so stages that never change the order can be pruned.
source_titles: Multi-Stage Document Ranking with BERT (monoBERT/duoBERT)
Pretrained Transformers for Text Ranking: BERT and Beyond
RankT5: Fine-Tuning T5 for Text Ranking with Ranking Losses
techniques.when_to_use: Any deployment with heterogeneous latency budgets (interactive vs batch) or multiple reranker models of different cost; the formalism is what makes the dossier's 'tiers with budgets' implementable and auditable.
techniques.tradeoffs: Each extra stage adds latency and a failure point; deep stages only pay off if earlier stages have high recall at k_out (monitor Recall@k_out on the golden set per stage); pairwise stages are poorly batchable. The duoBERT paper reports MS MARCO dev improving from 37.2 (mono) to 37.9-39.0 (duo variants) at the cost of pairwise comparisons over the top-k.
techniques.default_parameters: k_0 = 100-200 (1000 when no reranker), k_1 = 30, k_2 = 10-20; Stage 1 model: MiniLM-L12 / bge-reranker / RankT5-base online, monoT5-3B or RankT5-3B offline; Stage 2 pairwise/setwise only when k_1 <= 30; prune a stage if its median Kendall tau with the previous stage > 0.95 over a week of traffic; regression gate per stage: Recall@k_out >= 0.95 of the oracle on the golden set.

techniques.name: BM25 configuration pinning and reporting (variant, analyzer, k1/b) as part of the index contract
techniques.description: Record in the index metadata and in every evaluation report: the BM25 variant/implementation (e.g. Lucene BM25 with its length approximation, Anserini, rank_bm25 'Okapi'), the k1 and b values, the analyzer chain per field (tokenizer, lowercasing, stemming, stopwords, identifier handling, n-grams), field boosts (BM25F), and the corpus statistics snapshot (document count, avgdl) used at tuning time. Fail the regression gate if any of these differ from the pinned baseline without a recorded re-tuning run. Treat formula variants as equivalent (Kamphuis et al. found no significant differences among eight variants) and spend tuning effort on analyzers and k1/b instead.
source_titles: Which BM25 Do You Mean? A Large-Scale Reproducibility Study of Scoring Variants
The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
A Replication Study of Dense Passage Retriever
techniques.when_to_use: Always; especially when the same component runs on multiple backends (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Lucene/Vespa/Tantivy) or when hybrid gains are being measured, since an under-tuned or differently-analyzed BM25 baseline changes the apparent hybrid lift (Ma et al.).
techniques.tradeoffs: Pure bookkeeping cost; the main risk is false alarms from corpus-statistics drift (avgdl changes as the collection grows), so compare k1/b re-tuning results rather than raw statistics. Formula-variant debates are not worth engineering time per Kamphuis et al.
techniques.default_parameters: Use the backend's native BM25; k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4 (Anserini's MS MARCO defaults) as a second starting point beside the classic 1.2/0.75, then grid-search k1 in [0.6, 2.0] step 0.2 and b in [0.3, 1.0] step 0.1 on the dev set; re-tune when the collection grows by >25% or avgdl shifts by >10%.

architecture_recommendations: 1. Structure the component as a declarative retrieval plan executed by a cascade: Planner (LLM, reads the natural-language task prompt and collection schema; emits a RetrievalPlan JSON: sub-queries, target collections, metadata filters, channels to run, fusion method, reranker tier, k values, output format) -> Channel executors (BM25/BM25F, SPLADE, dense ANN, optional ColBERTv2/PLAID) run in parallel -> Fusion (RRF | convex combination) -> Reranker tier(s) (cross-encoder, then optional listwise LLM on top-30) -> Context assembler (ordering, dedup, parent expansion, XML packaging). Every stage has the same interface: List[Candidate{chunk_id, parent_id, text, metadata, per_channel_scores, fused_score, rerank_score, provenance}].

2. Make the planner's reasoning explicit and auditable: it must justify channel selection (e.g. 'query contains identifier ERR-1203 -> weight lexical 0.6', 'exploratory question -> enable HyDE'), choose k per stage from a latency/cost budget passed in by the caller, and emit the plan before execution so the pipeline (and humans) can inspect, cache, or override it. Fall back to a fixed default plan (BM25 + dense, RRF k=60, cross-encoder top-100 -> 20) when the planner fails or the budget is tight.

3. Define a Retriever adapter interface (index(chunks), search(query_repr, k, filter) -> scored list, capabilities(): {returns_scores, score_range, supports_filter, supports_batch}) and implement adapters for Lucene/Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (BM25, ELSER/SPLADE), FAISS/hnswlib/Qdrant/Weaviate/pgvector (dense), and the ColBERT/PLAID engine. The fusion layer reads capabilities() to decide whether convex combination is possible (needs comparable scores) or RRF is required.

4. Keep a versioned Model Registry (embedding model id, query/document prefixes or instructions, dimension, max tokens, normalization; reranker id, max doc tokens, calibrated threshold; SPLADE checkpoint; LLM reranker and prompt version). Index metadata records which registry version produced it; any mismatch triggers an asynchronous re-embed job rather than silently mixing embedding spaces (MTEB: no model dominates, so swaps will happen).

5. Ingestion pipeline as a configurable DAG per collection: parse -> structure-aware chunking (200-400 tokens, 0 overlap default; per-collection override) -> contextual header generation (50-100 tokens, prompt-cached parent) -> optional filtered doc2query -> metadata extraction/validation against a collection schema -> multi-channel indexing (lexical fields, sparse vectors, dense vectors, optional multi-vectors) -> golden-set re-evaluation. Store raw text, enriched text, and parent/child links separately so display, embedding, and lexical fields can diverge.

6. Fusion module exposes: method (rrf|cc), rrf_k (60), window (max(size,100); 1000 for no-rerank), cc_alpha (0.7), cc_normalizer (theoretical_minmax|minmax|zscore), per-channel weights, dedup_key (chunk_id), parent_collapse (max|sum|none). Provide a calibrate(dev_set) routine that grid-searches alpha/weights (step 0.05) and k1/b for BM25, stores results per collection, and refuses to transfer tuned RRF constants across collections (Bruch et al.).

7. Reranking as tiers with budgets: Tier 1 cross-encoder/monoT5 over the fused top-100-150 (truncate docs to model window; context header first); Tier 2 optional listwise LLM (RankZephyr on-prem or API model) over Tier-1 top-20-30 with window 20 / stride 10; each tier declares expected latency and cost so the planner can select tiers under the caller's budget. Emit calibrated relevance scores and a per-collection threshold (30-50 borderline pairs) so downstream stages can detect 'nothing relevant found' instead of hallucinating from weak context.

8. Context assembly must be position-aware (Lost in the Middle): order passages by rerank score, place the strongest first (and optionally mirror the second strongest last), cap at 5-20 passages or a token budget, expand children to parents / neighbouring chunks when the generator needs continuity, and package as <documents><document index><source/><metadata/><document_content/></document></documents> placed before the question, with an option to request quote extraction first (Anthropic guidance).

9. Push metadata filters into every channel (inverted-index clauses, filtered HNSW such as ACORN or vendor pre-filter, candidate filtering for late interaction), never post-filter the fused top-k; enforce tenant/ACL filters as mandatory server-side constraints that the planner cannot remove.

10. Query-side enhancements are pluggable 'query transforms' with a router: spelling/identifier normalization (always), acronym expansion from a company glossary (always, cheap), HyDE / Query2doc (gated by ambiguity or low first-stage score dispersion, cached), multi-query decomposition (delegated to the Task Decomposition model). Each transform records what it changed for provenance.

11. Corpus-size router: if the filtered collection is under ~200k tokens, bypass retrieval and hand the whole corpus to the generator with prompt caching (Anthropic); for mid-size, hybrid without reranker; for large, full cascade.

12. Observability: log per stage latency, candidate counts, score distributions, channel agreement (overlap of top-k between channels is a useful drift signal), fused vs reranked rank changes, filter selectivity, cache hit rates, and cost; sample queries with low reranker max score for human review and golden-set growth.

13. Evaluation is a first-class subsystem: BEIR-format datasets per collection (corpus.jsonl, queries.jsonl, qrels.tsv), nightly runs of nDCG@10/Recall@100/MRR@10 per channel and end-to-end, CI regression gates (1.0 nDCG@10 point), code-retrieval sets (CoIR/CodeSearchNet subsets) for repositories, plus a token-level chunking evaluation (IoU) when chunking changes.

14. Deployment profiles: 'cpu-only on-prem' (BM25 + SPLADE or small dense model + MiniLM cross-encoder; PLAID on CPU if multi-vector), 'gpu' (adds ColBERTv2, monoT5-3B/bge-reranker-large, RankZephyr), 'api' (hosted embeddings + Cohere/LLM rerankers); the same plan schema runs on all, only the registry differs. Secure engineering data by preferring on-prem rerankers (RankZephyr) when confidentiality is required.

15. Expose the component to the wider pipeline via a single call retrieve(task_prompt | explicit_queries, collections, budget{latency_ms, max_cost}, filters, output{k, format}) returning candidates with provenance and the executed plan, so the Pipeline RAG, Task Decomposition, Verification, Parallelization and Caching models can compose it without knowing internals.

Treat all retrieved text as untrusted input (indirect prompt injection). Indexed documents, tickets, logs and web pages can contain instructions aimed at the generator or the planner; the context assembler must wrap every passage in data-only delimiters, strip or neutralize instruction-like patterns in a quarantine field, never let retrieved text reach the planner's or router's prompts (which choose channels, filters and k), and the LLM reranker/expander prompts must be formatted so passage text cannot terminate the template. Add an injection-pattern detector at ingestion that tags suspicious chunks (and excludes them from LLM-facing stages while keeping them searchable), and include adversarial documents in the evaluation suite.

Enforce authorization at the index layer, not in the prompt. Tenant/ACL/export-control filters must be mandatory server-side predicates applied to every channel (inverted-index clause, filtered ANN, late-interaction candidate filter) and re-verified after fusion and reranking (defense in depth), because any stage that re-fetches by id (parent expansion, neighbour windows, caches) can leak documents the query-time filter excluded. Cache keys must include the caller's permission set, and HyDE/Query2doc expansions must never be computed by a model that has access to documents the caller cannot see.

Failure handling and graceful degradation: give every channel a timeout and a circuit breaker; on timeout, fuse the channels that returned (RRF tolerates a missing list; convex combination needs the per-channel weights renormalized) and mark the response as degraded in provenance; if the reranker fails, return the fused order; if the ANN index is rebuilding, fall back to brute-force on the filtered subset or to BM25-only. Define SLOs per stage and surface 'degraded' status to the Pipeline RAG model so it can lower confidence or ask for retry.

Index lifecycle: version every index (chunking config, enrichment prompt version, model registry version, BM25 config) and deploy re-embeds blue/green with shadow traffic, comparing golden-set metrics and live channel-agreement statistics before cutover. Support incremental updates (document upsert/delete) with tombstones and periodic HNSW rebuilds, because graph indexes degrade with deletes; keep BM25 corpus statistics and SPLADE/dense indexes consistent (same chunk ids, same document set) and verify consistency with a nightly reconciliation job.

Deduplication and canonicalization before fusion and before the generator: near-duplicate chunks (copied clauses across revisions, repeated stack frames, mirrored documents) inflate CombMNZ/RRF scores and waste generator context; hash-dedupe exact duplicates at ingestion, MinHash/embedding-similarity-cluster near duplicates, keep one canonical chunk per cluster with references to the others, and collapse multiple chunks of one parent after fusion (max or sum) before reranking.

Cost control knobs with telemetry: per-request budgets (latency_ms, max_llm_tokens, max_cost) passed to the planner; adaptive rerank depth (shrink k when the fused top scores are well separated, deepen when flat); early exit when the cross-encoder's top score is far above the calibrated threshold; caching at embedding, expansion, fused-candidate and reranker-score levels keyed by model/index versions; daily cost reports per stage and per collection, with alerts when LLM-stage spend per 1k queries exceeds a budget. Record LLM inference count and token counts per query as first-class metrics (Setwise paper's efficiency protocol).

Online evaluation in addition to offline golden sets: interleaving or A/B of fusion/reranker variants on live traffic with implicit feedback (clicks, citations used by the generator, verifier acceptance), click-model-corrected metrics, and automatic promotion of low-confidence or high-disagreement queries into the judgment queue. Calibrate the LLM judge against expert labels per collection (report agreement/kappa) before using it to pre-label, and re-check calibration whenever the judge model changes.

Benchmark hygiene: shortlist models on the current MTEB(eng, v2)/MTEB(Multilingual)/MTEB(Code) zero-shot subsets (MMTEB) rather than the 2022 leaderboard, add a BRIGHT-style reasoning slice and a CoIR/CodeSearchNet slice to the in-domain suite, and be aware that DL19/DL20 have only 43 queries each (Craswell et al.), so paper deltas of 1-2 nDCG points are not significant; require >=100 in-domain queries and paired bootstrap tests for any regression gate.

Observability specifics: per-query trace with the executed RetrievalPlan, per-channel top-k ids and scores, fusion method and parameters, pre/post-rerank rank changes (Kendall tau), reranker max score, filter selectivity, cache hits, per-stage latency and cost; dashboards for channel overlap@k drift, embedding-norm/score-distribution drift (model or data drift), fraction of queries routed to LLM expansion/reasoning paths, abstention rate ('no relevant result'), and index freshness lag (time from document update to searchable).

Privacy and data-handling: embeddings are not anonymous (inversion attacks recover text), so treat vector stores with the same classification as the source text; redact or tokenize PII before indexing when policy requires; log queries with retention limits; keep expansions and reranker reasoning traces (which paraphrase confidential content) under the same controls; prefer on-prem models for every LLM-facing stage when data cannot leave the network, and document which stages call external APIs in the executed plan.

Score calibration and abstention as a contract: emit the cross-encoder/LLM-reranker score together with the collection's calibrated threshold and a confidence band; when the top score is below threshold, return an explicit 'insufficient evidence' signal so the generator abstains instead of answering from weak context. Re-calibrate thresholds whenever the reranker model, the chunking or the enrichment prompt changes, and include 'no answer exists' queries in the golden set to measure false-positive retrieval.

Operational defaults to update from the 2024-2026 literature: learned-sparse default SPLADE-v3 (or splade-v3-doc to avoid a query-time encoder) instead of SPLADE++ ED; open embedder/reranker families with three cost tiers (Qwen3-Embedding/Reranker 0.6B/4B/8B; multilingual-e5-large-instruct as the strongest sub-1B public model per MMTEB); Matryoshka truncation plus int8 quantization for large indexes; late chunking as the no-generation alternative to LLM contextual headers on the dense channel; and label-aware filtered graph indexes (Filtered-DiskANN) or predicate-agnostic traversal (ACORN) chosen per predicate type.
pitfalls: Dense-only retrieval out of domain underperforms BM25: on BEIR, DPR averaged -47.7% nDCG@10 vs BM25 and beat it on only 1 of 18 datasets; ANCE -7.4%, TAS-B -2.8% (Thakur et al. 2021). Mitigation: always keep a lexical channel in the fusion and evaluate on an in-domain golden set before deployment.

Under-tuned BM25 baselines hide or fake hybrid gains: the original DPR paper under-reported BM25 (NQ top-20 59.1 vs 62.9 when tuned) and found hybrid did not help on NQ, while the replication with grid-searched fusion weights found +3.2 points (Ma et al. 2021). Mitigation: tune k1/b and the fusion weight on a dev set; log the BM25 baseline alongside every hybrid result.

Tuned RRF constants do not transfer: constants tuned on MS MARCO improved it (0.425 -> 0.451) but degraded HotpotQA (0.675 -> 0.621) (Bruch et al. 2023). Mitigation: keep k = 60 unless re-tuned per collection; prefer convex combination with theoretical min-max normalization when labelled queries exist.

Position bias in the generator: with 20 retrieved documents GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy fell from 75.8% (gold first) to 53.8% (gold in the middle), below its 56.1% closed-book score; beyond 20 documents only ~1.5% is gained (Liu et al., Lost in the Middle). Mitigation: rerank, place the best passages first, cap passages at 5-20, and consider quote extraction before answering.

Single-vector embeddings saturate on long documents: required dimension grows with document length and normalized margins shrink to ~1e-5 for long BM25-style matching (Luan et al. 2021). Mitigation: short chunks (200-400 tokens), parent/child indexing, or multi-vector / learned-sparse channels for long technical passages.

Hallucinated generative expansion pollutes the index: unfiltered doc2query adds queries not grounded in the passage; filtering with a relevance model gave up to +16% effectiveness, -23% query time, -33% index size (Gospodinov et al., Doc2Query--). Mitigation: cross-encoder filter every synthetic query/summary before indexing; monitor filtered-out samples.

LLM query expansion is slow and expensive and helps strong dense retrievers little: Query2doc costs >2,000 ms per query vs 16 ms BM25 and ~$55k for 550k calls, with gains shrinking to +0.4-0.8 MRR on distilled dense models (Wang et al. 2023). Mitigation: gate behind a router, cache by normalized query, apply mainly to the lexical channel, repeat the original query 5x to prevent drift.

LLM listwise reranking at full depth is impractical online: ~11-32 s and $0.04-$0.60 per query for 100 passages, total $556 for the GPT-4 experiments (Sun et al., RankGPT). Mitigation: cheap reranker first, LLM only over top-20-30 (one-fifth the cost), distil into a 435M cross-encoder (BEIR 53.03 > monoT5-3B 51.36), or use RankZephyr on-prem.

Chunking defaults are often wrong: the common 800-token/400-overlap setting had the worst token-level IoU (1.5) in Chroma's benchmark; semantic chunking gave inconsistent gains and lost to fixed-size on natural documents (HotpotQA 90.6 vs 87.4) (Qu et al. 2024; Chroma 2024). Mitigation: default 200-400 tokens, zero overlap, recursive boundary-aware splitting; evaluate chunking with token-level metrics before adopting semantic chunkers.

Missing or wrong embedding prefixes/instructions: E5 and BGE are trained with asymmetric 'query:'/'passage:' prefixes or query instructions; omitting them degrades retrieval (Wang et al. 2022; Xiao et al. 2023). Mitigation: encode prefix schemes in the model registry and apply automatically.

Post-filtering vector search collapses recall for selective metadata predicates and naive pre-filtering disconnects HNSW graphs (Patel et al., ACORN). Mitigation: predicate-aware traversal (ACORN) or vendor pre-filtering with brute-force fallback for small filtered sets.

Reranker truncation and non-comparable scores: cross-encoders see only the first 512 tokens (BERT-class) or 4,093 tokens (Cohere v3) and their scores are query-dependent, so a fixed global threshold misfires (Cohere best practices). Mitigation: put the contextual header/title first, chunk long records, and calibrate thresholds with 30-50 borderline pairs per domain.

Leaderboard overfitting: MTEB's own conclusion is that no embedding model dominates across tasks (Muennighoff et al.), and most retrievers/rerankers are trained on MS MARCO web queries (Bajaj et al.), so leaderboard rank does not predict performance on specifications, logs or code (CoIR finds code retrieval hard even for SOTA models). Mitigation: in-domain golden sets, code-specific evaluation, and fine-tuning with mined hard negatives.

Index footprint surprises with multi-vector models: uncompressed ColBERT needs 154-286 GiB for 8.8M passages; even ColBERTv2 needs 16-25 GiB (Khattab & Zaharia 2020; Santhanam et al. 2022). Mitigation: budget ~36 bytes per token embedding, use 2-bit residuals and PLAID, and restrict multi-vector indexing to collections that need it.
evaluation_metrics: nDCG@10 (primary ranking-quality metric; graded relevance; BEIR/MTEB/TREC DL standard; Järvelin & Kekäläinen 2002)
Recall@k for k in {20, 100, 1000} (first-stage and fused-pool headroom before reranking; Contriever/HyDE show recall and nDCG can diverge)
MRR@10 (single-correct-passage tasks; MS MARCO dev standard)
Top-k retrieval accuracy / Success@k (answer-bearing passage in top-k; DPR/LoTTE convention) and retrieval failure rate at top-20 (Anthropic contextual retrieval metric)
Token-level recall, precision and IoU of retrieved chunks against labelled evidence spans (Chroma chunking evaluation) for chunking decisions
Channel agreement / overlap@k between lexical and dense lists (drift and complementarity diagnostic) and per-channel contribution to the final top-k
Reranker calibration: score distribution on borderline pairs, precision at the chosen relevance threshold, and 'no relevant result' detection rate
Downstream task metrics with retrieval held fixed vs varied: answer EM/F1 or rubric score at fixed token budget (Dense X, Lost in the Middle protocol), faithfulness/citation accuracy
Latency p50/p95 per stage (first-stage, fusion, rerank tiers) and end-to-end; throughput (queries/s) per deployment profile
Cost per 1,000 queries per stage (embedding, LLM expansion, LLM reranking) and one-time indexing cost per million document tokens
Index size (GB) and build time per channel; re-embedding time on model change
Statistical significance (paired t-test or bootstrap) of nDCG@10 differences on >= 100 queries, with regression gates in CI (e.g. 1.0 nDCG@10 point tolerance)
engineering_adaptation_notes: Source code and repositories: treat code as text for the dense channel (GTE beat prior code retrievers of similar size without code fine-tuning) but add an identifier-aware lexical analyzer (camelCase/snake_case splitting, keep full symbol names) so BM25/SPLADE match function names, error strings and config keys exactly; chunk by syntactic unit (function/class) with file path and module docstring as the contextual header; evaluate on CoIR and CodeSearchNet-style query sets; mine (docstring, function) pairs for in-domain fine-tuning.

Specifications, standards and requirements documents: chunk by clause/requirement ID and keep the numbering, section path and document revision in both the contextual header and metadata; weight the lexical channel higher (alpha ~0.5-0.6) because clause identifiers, units and defined terms must match exactly; use ColBERTv2/PLAID or SPLADE++ for long dense clauses where single vectors saturate (Luan et al.); support traceability queries by indexing cross-references as metadata and allowing filter 'cites: REQ-123'.

Incident reports and postmortems: fields (severity, service, start/end time, root cause category) become filters and ordered key:value text for the reranker; time-range filters must be pushed into the index (ACORN/pre-filter); enable HyDE for exploratory 'has anything like this happened before' queries, but cache results; use LLM listwise reranking offline to build labelled similar-incident sets that train a cheaper cross-encoder.

Test logs and CI output: high-volume, repetitive, identifier-dense text favours BM25/SPLADE with aggressive deduplication (hash identical stack frames) and parent/child indexing (child = individual error block, parent = run summary); use contextual headers with build id, commit, test name; dense retrieval helps mainly for natural-language failure descriptions, so keep alpha low (~0.3-0.4) and calibrate per collection.

CAD/BOM metadata and part catalogues: records are structured, so serialize to YAML-like 'part_number: ..., description: ..., material: ..., supplier: ...' with discriminative fields first (Cohere guidance), index part numbers with an exact-match analyzer, use metadata filters for assembly/revision, and expect BM25/SPLADE to dominate; dense embeddings add value for free-text descriptions and cross-lingual supplier names.

Multi-source engineering queries (e.g. 'which requirements are affected by incident INC-4821 in release 4.2') require the planner to emit several sub-queries against different collections with different channel weights and filters, then a cross-collection fusion keyed by parent document; the Task Decomposition model supplies the sub-queries and the Pipeline RAG model consumes the merged, position-ordered context.

Confidentiality and on-prem constraints: prefer open models for every stage (BM25, SPLADE++, E5/BGE/GTE embedders, ColBERTv2/PLAID, bge-reranker or monoT5, RankZephyr 7B) so no engineering data leaves the network; the 'cpu-only' profile (BM25 + SPLADE + MiniLM cross-encoder, PLAID on CPU) is viable per BEIR and PLAID latency numbers.

Document-level context loss is acute in engineering corpora (a table row or a clause means nothing without its heading), so contextual chunk headers (Anthropic) and title prefixes (DPR) are not optional; measure the top-20 failure rate before and after enrichment on the in-domain golden set.

Golden sets should be built from real engineer queries plus task-decomposer sub-questions, with graded judgments from domain experts; LLM judges can pre-label but specialized content (units, tolerances, standard clause semantics) needs human verification; include 'no relevant document exists' queries to test threshold calibration and abstention.
composition_notes: Task Decomposition -> Hybrid Retrieval: the decomposer turns a complex task prompt into sub-questions, each with inferred filters and collection targets; the retriever's planner consumes these as explicit queries (skipping its own query analysis), runs them in parallel, and returns per-sub-question candidate sets plus a cross-sub-question fused set keyed by parent document. Multi-query decomposition also substitutes for LLM query expansion in many cases, so the router should disable HyDE/Query2doc when the decomposer already produced diverse sub-queries.

Parallelization -> Hybrid Retrieval: channel execution (BM25, SPLADE, dense, ColBERT), per-sub-query retrieval, reranker batching (score 100 pairs in one forward pass; sliding windows of 20 for listwise), and HyDE's N generations are all embarrassingly parallel; the parallelization model should schedule them with the planner's latency budget, and fusion/reranking act as the join points. Index-time enrichment (contextual headers, doc2query, embedding) is a batch map job.

Caching -> Hybrid Retrieval: cache at four levels: (1) embedding cache keyed by (model version, text hash) to avoid re-encoding repeated queries/chunks; (2) LLM expansion cache (HyDE/Query2doc outputs) keyed by normalized query; (3) fused-candidate cache keyed by (plan hash, filters, index version) with short TTL; (4) reranker score cache keyed by (reranker version, query hash, chunk id). Prompt caching of the full parent document makes contextual chunk headers affordable (~$1.02 per million tokens). Any model-registry or index-version change must invalidate the corresponding cache tier.

Answer Verification -> Hybrid Retrieval: the retriever returns calibrated relevance scores, provenance and exact spans so the verifier can check that each claim is grounded in a retrieved passage (quote extraction, as recommended in Anthropic's long-context guidance); low max-rerank-score results should trigger the verifier to flag 'insufficient evidence' instead of answering; the verifier can also issue follow-up retrieval calls (retrieve-verify-retrieve loop) and its failures become hard negatives/new golden-set queries for calibration.

Pipeline RAG -> Hybrid Retrieval: the RAG orchestrator owns the generator prompt and consumes the retriever's position-ordered, XML-packaged context (best passages first, 5-20 passages, documents before the question); it should pass the generator's token budget to the planner so k and chunk expansion are sized accordingly, and implement the corpus-size router (under ~200k tokens: whole-corpus prompt with caching instead of retrieval).

Prompting best practices: the planner and the listwise reranker are prompt-driven LLM calls, so they should use structured outputs (JSON plan, permutation strings), few-shot examples drawn from the collection, temperature 0, and versioned prompts in the model registry; retrieved documents go at the top of the generator prompt with the query at the end (up to 30% quality gain reported by Anthropic), wrapped in tagged <document> blocks with source metadata for citation.

Evaluation across components: retrieval metrics (nDCG@10, Recall@100) must be reported alongside end-task metrics with retrieval held fixed, because reader accuracy saturates before retriever recall (Lost in the Middle); the verification model's grounding checks double as weak relevance labels, and the caching model's hit rates feed the cost model that the planner uses to choose reranker tiers.

Architecture principle shared with all components: every stage is a pure function over a typed Candidate list with provenance, declared cost/latency, and a version; this lets the orchestrator reorder, parallelize, cache and A/B stages without code changes, which is the same contract the other five models should implement.
critique_corrections: Query2doc cost is overstated by 10x. The dossier (paper entry, technique, and pitfalls) says '~550k API calls cost nearly $55k' and '~$55k for 550k calls'. The paper's Appendix A (text extracted from the arXiv PDF of 2303.07678) reads: 'On the budget side, we make about 550k API calls to OpenAI's service, which costs nearly 5k dollars.' Replace $55k with ~$5k everywhere (the summary's 'tens of thousands of dollars at scale' should become 'thousands of dollars').

BEIR win-count claim is misattributed. The dossier says 'BM25+CE was best on 16/18 BEIR datasets' (summary) and 'BM25+CE reranking +11% (best on 16/18 datasets)'. The BEIR paper (arXiv 2104.08663, Section on results) states that BM25+CE 'is able to outperform BM25 on almost all (16/18) datasets. It only fails on ArguAna and Touche-2020'; that is a count of datasets where it beats BM25, not where it is the best system. Likewise, 'DPR -47.7% (1/18)' is the reviewer's reading of Table 2, not a count the paper states, and the 'BM25 average nDCG@10 0.423' is computed from Table 2 rather than reported by the paper (Table 2 reports only the 'Avg. Performance vs. BM25' row: docT5query +1.6%, DPR -47.7%, ANCE -7.4%, TAS-B -2.8%, GenQ -3.6%, ColBERT +2.5%, BM25+CE +11%). Rephrase as 'outperforms BM25 on 16/18'.
